name: Oxymetazoline eye drops (Upneeq)

card.summary: A prescription 0.1% oxymetazoline eye drop approved for acquired ptosis that lifts the lid slightly; forum users discuss cheaper nasal-spray substitutes, which are not the approved product.
card.note: Nasal-spray substitutes are not the approved eye formulation; ask a clinician.

quick.overview:
Upneeq is oxymetazoline hydrochloride 0.1% ophthalmic solution, approved by the FDA in July 2020 for acquired blepharoptosis in adults. Oxymetazoline is also long used in nasal decongestant sprays and redness eye drops.

Its appearance use is a brief lift of a mildly drooping upper lid for a more open look. On looksmax.org, users have asked whether nasal spray can substitute because Upneeq is costly and hard to obtain in Europe.
quick.mechanism: Oxymetazoline is an alpha-adrenergic agonist; for ptosis it is thought to stimulate receptors in Muller's muscle, which raises the lid.
quick.risks: Wikipedia describes rebound congestion and dependence with nasal oxymetazoline. Nasal spray is formulated for the nose, and clinicians' views on its use in the eye are not covered by the sources reviewed.

lead: Upneeq is a brand of 0.1% oxymetazoline hydrochloride ophthalmic solution, approved by the US FDA in July 2020 to treat acquired blepharoptosis (drooping of the upper eyelid).[5] Oxymetazoline is an imidazole-derivative alpha-adrenergic agonist developed from xylometazoline at Merck in 1961, and is also used in nasal sprays, redness drops and a rosacea cream.[5]

For ptosis, the drug is thought to act on alpha receptors in Muller's muscle to lift the lid.[5] It is also used, in published case reports, to manage eyelid ptosis after botulinum toxin treatment.[1]
In looksmaxxing forums, Upneeq is discussed as a way to get a more open eye without surgery, and users discuss its cost and availability outside the US.[6]

paras: Approved use is acquired blepharoptosis in adults.[5] Published reports describe oxymetazoline 0.1% together with pretarsal botulinum toxin for severe botulinum-induced ptosis.[1] Wikipedia lists other oxymetazoline uses as nasal decongestion, eye redness and facial redness in rosacea.[5]
Oxymetazoline mainly activates alpha-1 and partly alpha-2 adrenergic receptors; in ptosis these actions in Muller's muscle are thought to elevate the lid.[5]

For nasal oxymetazoline, Wikipedia reports rebound congestion and describes a moderate dependence liability, with a 2006 review recommending limiting nasal use to three days.[5] Ophthalmic adverse-event data were not found in the sources reviewed.

A looksmax.org poster said that Upneeq is very expensive and nearly impossible to obtain in Europe, and asked whether a nasal spray seen used as eye drops on Reddit could serve as an alternative and whether this would be safe.[6]

Registered trials include a completed Phase 4 study of Upneeq on eyelid position, eye redness and appearance (NCT04831047, 114 participants),[2] a completed Phase 3 trial of oxymetazoline for ptosis from synkinesis (NCT05945615, 36 participants),[3] and a planned Phase 4 comparison of Upneeq and Lumify for ptosis (NCT07390578).[4] A published report describes oxymetazoline for botulinum-induced ptosis.[1]

timeline.event: Oxymetazoline is developed at Merck (per Wikipedia).[5]
FDA approves 1% oxymetazoline cream for rosacea (per Wikipedia).[5]
FDA approves oxymetazoline 0.1% ophthalmic solution for acquired blepharoptosis.[5]

lore.intro: Discussion centres on cost, availability and whether nasal sprays can be substituted.[6]

claims.claim: A nasal spray can be used as an alternative to Upneeq eye drops.
claims.believers: A poster says Upneeq is expensive and hard to get in Europe and cites a Reddit user using nasal spray as drops.[6]
claims.experts: No published studies of nasal spray in the eye were found in the sources reviewed; the approved product is a dedicated ophthalmic solution.[5]
